A1-A2.headline: How Cities and Climate Change Connect

pages.text:
Big cities and world weather have a close link. The United Nations thinks 68% of all people will live in cities by 2050.

Medium cities with 500,000 to one million people are growing fast and changing nature around them.
pages.caption: Jakarta is a major city facing climate changes.

evidence.articleCaption: Jakarta was listed as the most vulnerable city to climate change in a 2021 Verisk Maplecroft study.

pages.text:
Around the world, cities hold half of all people, use 80% of all power, and make over 70% of carbon gas. Still, tracking where that gas starts takes real care.

A report from the C40 Cities group says 85% of gas tied to city goods is actually made outside city borders, where food and items are built.

Long ago, people built towns beside rivers and warm coasts. Because of that, modern cities now face strong weather risks every year.

Rising seas threaten coast roads and homes with heavy water and lost soil. Local trouble like dry underground water and hot city streets makes these problems even worse.

Solving these nature risks needs smart plans and fast action. Packing homes closer together saves open land, helps public buses and trains run well, and keeps buildings safe from hard weather.

With strong world rules and smart local plans, cities can change from big waste makers into leaders for a clean future.

B1-B2.headline: Urban Centers and the Global Climate Challenge

pages.text:
Urban areas and climate change share a close, complex link. The United Nations projects that 68% of humanity will live in cities by 2050.

Mid-sized cities of 500,000 to one million residents are growing fast, reshaping local impacts.
pages.caption: Jakarta is listed as a highly vulnerable city.

evidence.articleCaption: Jakarta was listed as the most vulnerable city to climate change in a 2021 Verisk Maplecroft study.

pages.text:
Worldwide, cities house half of humanity, consume 80% of total energy, and generate over 70% of carbon dioxide emissions. Yet tracing exact sources takes careful accounting.

A report by the C40 Cities group estimates that 85% of emissions linked to urban consumer goods are actually produced outside city borders.

Because historic towns grew beside rivers and coasts, modern cities face growing climate threats. Rising sea levels endanger coastal transport and housing, causing severe flooding and soil loss.

These coastal dangers are worsened by local strains such as shrinking underground water supplies and intense urban heat islands.

Meeting these climate pressures demands practical planning and bold action. Higher city density supports better land use, strong public transit systems, and weather-ready buildings.

Through joined global policies and local urban design, cities can shift from major sources of pollution into vital engines of green growth.

C1-C2.headline: Urban Metabolism, Emissions Accounting, and Resilient Adaptation

pages.text:
Urbanization and climate change maintain an intricate, reciprocal relationship. United Nations forecasts project 68% of humanity inhabiting cities by 2050.

Secondary cities of 500,000 to one million rapidly reshape regional ecology.
pages.caption: Jakarta exemplifies severe urban climate vulnerability.

evidence.articleCaption: Jakarta was listed as the most vulnerable city to climate change in a 2021 Verisk Maplecroft study.

pages.text:
Globally, metropolitan centers accommodate half of humanity, consume 80% of aggregate energy, and account for over 70% of carbon dioxide output. Pinpointing precise provenance nonetheless requires rigorous accounting.

Research by the C40 Cities consortium estimates 85% of emissions embedded within urban consumption originate beyond municipal boundaries.

Because historical settlements gravitated toward rivers and coastlines, contemporary metropolises confront acute climatic hazards. Accelerating sea-level rise imperils coastal infrastructure, precipitating severe inundation and shoreline erosion.

Localized stressors—including subterranean aquifer depletion and urban heat island amplification—further compound these vulnerabilities.

Confronting these environmental pressures demands integrated adaptation alongside proactive mitigation. Compact density enables efficient land allocation, transit corridors, and resilient buildings.

Through coordinated international policies and municipal governance, cities can transition from major emitters into catalysts for global sustainability.
